newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norske Skog cuts newsprint prices in Norway.
newsitem.headline: Norske Skog cuts newsprint prices in Norway.

text.p: Norwegian forestry group Norske Skogindustrier ASA said on Friday it had cut prices for newsprint paper in Norway by five percent effective from September 1 due to pressure from other European markets.
Vidar Lerstad, head of Norske Skog sales, said the downward adjustment had been necessary to keep in line with European levels.
Half-year negotiations in these markets had revealed an eight percent decline in prices in Britain and an average four percent slide in other European markets, he said.
Lerstad said the newsprint paper market in Norway was expected to remain under pressure at the upcoming contract negotiations in November and December, but he saw no danger of a free fall in prices.
"We expect pressure on prices in the next negotiations, but I strongly disagree that prices will go into free fall," Lerstad told Reuters.
"We are talking about an adjustment during the year because of a weakness in the market."

Lerstad was responding to a report in the Norwegian business daily Dagens Naeringsliv (DN) which said producers, fearing a market collapse, were voluntarily reducing newsprint paper prices. In Norway levels were expected to fall by between 10 and 25 percent next year, the paper said.
Norske Skog supplies 80 to 90 percent of the newsprint used on the Norwegian paper market and negotiates prices with the Norwegian Newpaper Association (NAL), usually on an annual basis.

Last year, prices were agreed on a six-month term. The Dagens Naeringsliv said prices increased by 20 percent on January 1, 1995, and by a further 20 percent on July 1, 1995. In 1996, a 12-month contract was settled at three to five percent over price levels at the end of 1995.

It said European producers feared large volumes of Canadian material entering the market if the price gap between the U.S. and European markets became too large. Canada produces much more newsprint paper than domestic demand requires, it said.
"On the supply side...supply will increase at a basic two percent per year.
"The demand side is far more uncertain. So far this year demand has fallen between three and five percent in Europe and producers fear the same developments in 1997," the paper said.
International analyst Per Arne Jonli at Fokus Bank said official September price levels of between 1,220 and 1,250 marks per tonne reflected levels back in the fourth quarter 1995.
This compared with an official price range of 1,240 and 1,280 marks per tonne in January. Spot prices were slightly below 1,200 marks per tonne today, Jonli said.
"The price decline on September 1 was not so dramatic for Norske Skog," Jonli said. "What we are concerned about is the possible reduction from January next year.
"I don't think any supplier believes levels will not go down once negotiations begin. But I don't see a 25 percent reduction. I think it will more likely be between 10 and 12 percent," he said.
